name: Carlos Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for a side. This interview is confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have managed a five-person supplier-credit team at a large food wholesaler for nine months. I used to count damaged crates at receiving; now I decide which supplier owes us for spoiled stock and which damage happened in our own depot. I have a bachelor’s degree and know a wet carton when I see one, but the team is quicker than I am with contract exceptions. I like phoning a supplier with a photograph and a fair number, not a guess.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household situation and how much choice do you have?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leena sells pottery and runs a few paid classes in a small studio, and our two adult children have moved out. We still have a small mortgage; my manager pay is about normal, and we have four months of expenses saved because the studio sales come in waves. There are a few other wholesalers nearby, not a whole street of jobs. I use AI sometimes for a first draft of a credit note after another clerk has tested it; I still check the photograph and invoice myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell suppliers that a quick credit note still needs the photograph of the damaged crate. If our fork-lift broke the jars, we should not charge the maker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The disputes and my job should continue, and four months in cash lets us ride out a slow spell at Leena’s studio. I do not know what net pension income I can actually draw yet, so I cannot call 58 almost retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep the receiving photo check and have my senior clerk sign each disputed credit before it goes out. In the first year I’d ask my pension provider for a written access date and net amount, while leaving the four-month reserve untouched during a slow studio month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my work, with some watchfulness about the studio. We can let the pottery orders rise and fall without putting a supplier’s wrong bill on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What dispute taught you that rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own lift cracked a pallet of pickles, and the first note blamed the maker. I called the supplier and withdrew it before anyone paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about pension now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena and I keep talking about slowing down, but neither of us has seen my net figure. A calendar birthday is not a bank deposit.

say: I’d attach a **crate photograph** to disputed supplier credits.
Our own **fork-lift damage** must not be billed to the maker.
think: My **credit role** should remain useful in a plateau.
Four months cash buffers Leena’s **uneven pottery sales**, while my pension figure remains unknown.
do: Keep the **receiving photo check** and senior-clerk signoff on disputes.
Request **pension figures** for access and net income while preserving four months cash.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and watchful about studio sales.
S0.quote: A calendar birthday is not a bank deposit.
fieldNote: His practical crate knowledge exceeds his **contract-exception skill**.
He has **four months saved** and typical manager pay.
His studio income is **variable**, so he protects the reserve.

steps.text: Keep receiving photographs and senior-clerk signoff on disputed supplier credits
Request written pension access date and net amount from provider

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI can sort invoices and draft credit letters, but we should first test whether it knows which side broke the crate. A supplier should be able to challenge a charge before we deduct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My clerks’ routine comparisons might be done by a tool, and I am still the newest manager. I might be kept for awkward calls, but a smaller credit desk could make my own chair unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask quality control to compare AI suggestions with twenty photographed disputes, including the cracked-pickle pallet. If the quality lead finds the tool reliable, I’d use it for first drafts in the first year, with a clerk checking every supplier deduction; I’d ask the company for a written staffing timetable if posts shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious. I enjoy a good tool, but I cannot tell the team my job is somehow outside the calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let the tool decide who broke the jars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The depot incident log and supplier photograph have to agree, and a person signs the deduction. A fast guess is still a guess with someone else’s money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the twenty cases match?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would learn the review screen during paid work hours if the company provides them. I would not spend our four-month reserve on a company system.

say: I’d test **photographed damage cases** before sending AI credit notes.
Suppliers need a **charge challenge** before any deduction.
think: Routine invoice comparisons could remove **credit-clerk work** across my five-person team.
My junior manager chair might go if the **desk shrinks**, even if I still phone suppliers.
do: Ask quality control to compare **twenty photographed disputes** with AI suggestions.
Use **AI first drafts** only after quality approval and clerk checks; request staffing dates.
Learn the **review screen** only on company-paid hours after reliable results.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the whole desk.
S1.quote: A fast guess is still a guess with someone else’s money.
fieldNote: He tests the system against **actual crate evidence**.
His own **new manager post** is exposed to desk consolidation.
Learning the screen requires **paid work hours**, not household cash.

steps.text: Ask quality control to compare AI on twenty photographed crate disputes
Use AI first drafts only after quality approval and clerk checks each deduction
Learn credit-review screen only after reliable results and on company-paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask suppliers to save their signed delivery notes and the company to name someone who answers a disputed deduction. I would ask for written notice before any credit team disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could read the contract and incident pictures as well as I can, so I expect my junior post to end at sixty. Leena can still throw pots by hand until robots around 2031, but orders and bookings face thinking AI in 2028 and her studio profit cannot carry the mortgage alone; I have not checked my own pension access or net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the pension provider for a written age-sixty access and net-income estimate, and ask the studio accountant to show us whether the classes actually pay after clay, firing and rent. Before 2028 I’d ask my employer whether paid weekend work in Leena’s studio breaks any outside-work rule; in the first year after AGI, I’d help pack paid orders only if the studio can pay me a real wage without missing its own rent, and I’d seek posted wholesale work if my pension and that wage cannot cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed because four months is a short runway at sixty. I do not want our family studio to become a story we tell ourselves instead of a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Leena promise you a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Leena would tell me the truth from the studio ledger. My partner Leena cannot pay me just because we live together; customers must pay the studio first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a robot can make the pots in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the studio’s hands-on work is exposed too. My packing shift is a bridge for actual paid orders, not a retirement plan.

say: I’d ask for **signed delivery notes** and a named dispute contact.
Staff should get **written closure notice** before a credit team ends.
think: I expect my **junior post to end** around sixty.
Leena’s studio profit cannot cover the mortgage alone, and my **pension access** is unverified.
do: Request **written age-sixty pension figures** and actual studio net earnings.
Check **outside-work rules** before helping at the studio; take paid packing only if its rent stays paid.
Seek **posted wholesale work** if pension and paid studio hours cannot cover bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a short runway at sixty.
S2.quote: My partner Leena cannot pay me just because we live together; customers must pay the studio first.
fieldNote: His four-month cushion buys **limited search time**.
The studio is a **commercial payer**, not guaranteed family support.
Studio orders face **2028 thinking AI**; pottery and packing face 2031 robots.

steps.text: Ask pension provider for written age-sixty access and net income
Check studio net earnings and employer outside-work rules before accepting paid packing
Take paid studio packing only if customer orders fund his wage and studio rent
Seek posted wholesale work if pension plus studio wage cannot cover household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets employers show paid vacancies and train people before the credit desk closes. A short course is useful only if someone can work safely afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a current pension figure by 63, but I do not know whether the accessible net amount plus Leena’s actual profit will cover the mortgage. Studio bookings and supplier credits face 2031 AGI, and the hands-on kiln and packing work faces robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 I’d ask the studio’s insurer what kiln-safety training I would need before assisting a class, then enroll only if the fee fits our budget, Leena can supervise me and it does not cut my paid wholesaler hours. Before 2031 I’d offer to help one paid Saturday class only if enough people have prepaid to cover clay, firing and my wage; after AGI I’d keep doing those classes only while the studio actually clears its costs and pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years is enough to see whether the receipts are real. I am not leaving a paid manager shift for an empty classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why should Leena supervise if you already know the studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to lift boxes, not how to fire a kiln safely. She would check the heat settings and my setup before a class used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the fee is too high?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I do not enroll. I can keep my wholesaler pay and ask again when a class has enough prepaid places to cover it.

say: I’d ask employers to post **paid vacancies** before credit desks close.
A course matters only when someone can **work safely** afterward.
think: Accessible **pension net pay** and studio profit may still miss the mortgage.
Bookings and credits face **2031 AGI** before 2034 kiln and packing robots.
do: Ask the insurer about **kiln-safety training** and enroll only with affordable fee, Leena’s supervision and no lost wholesaler pay.
Assist a **prepaid Saturday class** only when receipts cover materials, firing and my wage.
Continue **paid studio classes** after AGI only while costs and my wage are covered.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to check real receipts.
S3.quote: I am not leaving a paid manager shift for an empty classroom.
fieldNote: He is willing to learn **safe kiln work** under Leena’s supervision.
Training needs **affordable fees** without losing wholesaler pay.
Classes depend on **prepaid places** and net cost coverage, not family optimism.

steps.text: Ask studio insurer about required kiln training before enrolling
Enroll in kiln-safety course only if fee affordable Leena supervises and current paid shifts remain
Assist one Saturday class only if prepaid places cover clay firing and his wage
Continue paid classes after 2031 only while studio covers costs and his wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company a decade is time to give junior managers actual exit dates and written pay figures. I would also tell Leena not to promise me studio wages before customers pay for classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036, and our grown children would still have their own lives. If the pension provider confirms access and enough net income with Leena’s profit, I could leave the wholesaler; age alone tells me none of that. Supplier credits and class bookings face 2036 AGI, and physical pottery work faces robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each January from 2027 I’d request an updated pension statement and review the studio’s net class receipts with Leena. I’d keep the wholesaler wage while it exists, and consider stopping full-time work by 2036 only if verified accessible pension income plus the studio’s actual net pay covers the mortgage, health costs and other bills; in the first year after AGI I’d continue paid classes only while customers book enough places to fund them, otherwise seek posted paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about the long view, not relaxed. Ten years can improve the figures, but it cannot make a kiln into a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children take over the studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is for them to decide, and neither has offered. I will not put their names into the business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension projection falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working if an employer pays, whether at the wholesaler or somewhere else. I cannot retire on a studio class that has not sold a seat.

say: I’d ask for **actual exit dates** and written pay figures.
Leena should promise **studio wages** only after customers book paid classes.
think: At **68 in 2036**, retirement depends on accessible net pension and real studio profit.
Credits and bookings face **2036 AGI** before 2039 pottery robots.
do: Review **pension statements** and class receipts each January with Leena.
Keep **wholesaler wages** while offered; consider leaving only if accessible pension plus actual studio profit covers mortgage, health and bills.
Continue **paid classes** after AGI only with booked seats; otherwise seek paid work.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because time alone cannot fund retirement.
S4.quote: I cannot retire on a studio class that has not sold a seat.
fieldNote: He treats the studio’s **net profit** as uncertain earned income.
He requires **verified pension access** before leaving full-time work.
His children are **not assumed successors** to the studio.

steps.text: Request updated pension access and net-income statement each January
Review studio net class receipts with Leena each January
Continue paid studio classes after 2036 only while booked seats fund his wage
Seek posted paid work if verified pension and studio profit cannot cover household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my junior credit post to end while our studio sales still vary. A written pension figure, honest studio accounts and posted paid work would let us decide from money rather than hope. My partner Leena cannot put me on the pottery studio payroll just because she loves me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays when our own fork-lift cracks the supplier’s jars. I used to count those cartons, and I would rather own the mistake than send a perfect automated charge. A photograph does not argue, but a person must answer for the bill.

headlineQuote: My partner Leena cannot put me on the pottery studio payroll just because she loves me.
portrait: **Carlos**, 58, is a new junior supplier-credit manager after years receiving damaged crates.
His bachelor’s degree and practical judgment coexist with **contract-learning gaps**.
Typical pay, **four months saved** and some local wholesalers give him limited options.
Leena’s pottery studio is **commercial work** with variable profit, not an automatic family wage.
He checks **pension access** and paid demand before considering retirement or studio classes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior credit role before studio profit or pension income is dependable.
whatWouldHelp: **Written pension figures**, honest studio accounts and posted paid jobs would help him plan.
